satire_techniques.caution: The list must be real or exactly plausible, and it must end one item before the reader's patience does; a catalogue kept going for its own sake becomes the tedium it was describing.

satire_techniques.name: literalized euphemism
satire_techniques.definition: Taking an institution's own softening term and staging what it literally describes, so the euphemism has to bear its referent in the reader's presence.
satire_techniques.example: A short scene in which the workforce is, precisely and physically, right-sized.
satire_techniques.effect: Restores the meaning the vocabulary was designed to suppress, using nothing but the vocabulary itself.
satire_techniques.caution: Distinct from the joke-shaped literalization of a figure: here the point is not the incongruity but the exposure, and the piece fails if the reader laughs and forgets the term.

satire_techniques.name: the ingénu narrator
satire_techniques.definition: A guileless observer — traveller, child, foreigner, newcomer — who reports a society's arrangements accurately because they do not know which parts are supposed to be invisible.
satire_techniques.example: The new starter's account of why the two systems cannot see each other, which nobody has been able to say aloud for nine years.
satire_techniques.effect: Licenses the naive question the reader has also been holding, and makes familiar arrangements strange without the writer appearing to editorialize.
satire_techniques.register: satirical fiction, comic essay, first-week reportage
satire_techniques.caution: The naif must be consistently naive — a narrator who understands too much on one page and too little on the next is a device the reader can see being operated.

satire_techniques.name: the pseudonymous persona letter
satire_techniques.definition: Satire published in the voice and under the name of an invented correspondent with a stated position in the world — a draper, a widow, a concerned ratepayer — sustained across pieces.
satire_techniques.example: Four letters from a man who describes himself as the only person in the county who has read the entire tender document.
satire_techniques.effect: The invented standing does work the writer's own could not: an ordinary voice can say things a byline cannot, and the accumulation makes the persona quotable.
satire_techniques.register: periodical satire, columns, epistolary comic writing
satire_techniques.caution: In a media environment that circulates single paragraphs, a well-built persona will be quoted as a real person; the frame has to be recoverable from any extract that can travel.

satire_techniques.name: the mock document
satire_techniques.definition: A complete counterfeit of a real document type — minutes, a risk register, a terms-of-service page — presented without narrative frame and left to be read as the thing it imitates.
satire_techniques.example: The full text of a fire-safety policy for a building whose only exit is described, in clause nine, as decorative.
satire_techniques.effect: Delivers the satire in the reader's own encounter with the document, with no narrator standing between them and it.
satire_techniques.register: print and online satire, comic anthologies
satire_techniques.caution: The most detachable satiric form and therefore the most often mistaken for genuine; internal impossibility, not a disclaimer at the bottom, is what protects it.

satire_techniques.name: the satiric definition
satire_techniques.definition: A dictionary entry whose gloss states the word's operative rather than its official meaning, in the deadpan syntax of lexicography.
satire_techniques.example: Consultation, n. The interval between a decision and its announcement.
satire_techniques.effect: Compresses an entire critique into one sentence with a form that dares the reader to disagree with a dictionary.
satire_techniques.register: aphoristic satire, glossaries, comic reference writing
satire_techniques.caution: The form is addictive and its returns fall fast; a glossary of forty is a pamphlet of four good ones and thirty-six that show the writer enjoying himself.

satire_techniques.name: quotation as indictment
satire_techniques.definition: Reproducing the target's own words at length, exactly, with no commentary, in a context that makes them answer for themselves — Kraus's method.
satire_techniques.example: The full paragraph from the annual report, printed under the date of the closure it does not mention.
satire_techniques.effect: The reader convicts the target, and the writer has asserted nothing that can be disputed; the only editorial act was the choice to reprint.
satire_techniques.caution: Selection is still an argument: a quotation cut before the qualifying clause is contextomy, and the technique's whole authority depends on the extract being fair.

satire_techniques.name: silent juxtaposition
satire_techniques.definition: Placing two true items side by side — a statement and a date, a policy and a photograph, two sentences from the same speech — and adding nothing.
satire_techniques.example: The pay award, and beneath it the transcript of the hardship-fund debate from the same afternoon.
satire_techniques.effect: The inference happens in the white space between the items, where the reader owns it and the writer cannot be accused of having made it.
satire_techniques.caution: Only one inference may be available; if the pairing supports a second reading, the reader draws it and the writer has no way to intervene.

satire_techniques.name: catch-22 construction
satire_techniques.definition: Building a rule set whose clauses are individually reasonable and jointly inescapable, so that the absurdity is produced by the system rather than asserted about it.
satire_techniques.example: Appeals must be lodged by a representative, and representatives may only be appointed by someone whose appeal has been heard.
satire_techniques.effect: Demonstrates institutional irrationality as a structure the reader can trace, which no amount of description of it achieves.
satire_techniques.caution: The loop must close cleanly in two or three clauses; a reader who has to be walked through five steps has stopped finding it funny and started finding it explained.

satire_techniques.name: beast fable
satire_techniques.definition: Assigning the target's roles to animals whose conventional attributes carry the judgement, so a political argument can be conducted in a form nobody can be sued over.
satire_techniques.example: The negotiation between the herd and the granary, in which the granary is represented by the mice who live in it.
satire_techniques.effect: The species does the characterization instantly and the reader's attention goes to the structure of the situation rather than to the personalities.
satire_techniques.register: allegorical satire, verse fable, children's satire
satire_techniques.caution: Animal attributes are cultural and stale; a fable that relies on the fox being cunning has spent its only idea in the cast list.

satire_techniques.name: carnivalesque inversion
satire_techniques.definition: Turning the hierarchy upside down for the duration of the piece — the porter runs the board, the ledger is read out at the feast — so that the order's arbitrariness shows in its absence.
satire_techniques.example: A day in which the complaints are heard by the people who wrote the complaints procedure, in their own waiting room.
satire_techniques.effect: Makes the arrangement visible as an arrangement, which is what a hierarchy's ordinary operation prevents.
satire_techniques.register: comic fiction, festival and folk satire, institutional comedy
satire_techniques.caution: Inversion is licensed play and its politics are ambiguous — the world rights itself at the end, and a satire that stops there has staged a holiday rather than an argument.

satire_techniques.name: the satiric grotesque
satire_techniques.definition: Rendering the target through bodily excess, distortion and hybridity — the swollen, the leaking, the part-machine — so that disgust does work argument cannot.
satire_techniques.example: The board described as a single organism with nine mouths and one digestive tract.
satire_techniques.effect: Produces a physical revulsion that attaches to the target and survives the reader's forgetting the argument attached to it.
satire_techniques.caution: Grotesque imagery drawn from real bodies — size, illness, disability — stops being satire and becomes the thing it borrows from; the distortion has to be of the target's conduct, not of a body type.

satire_techniques.name: roman à clef targeting
satire_techniques.definition: Fictionalizing real people and events closely enough that informed readers can key the characters to their originals, while the fiction remains formally deniable.
satire_techniques.example: A novel set in an unnamed ministry whose four principals correspond, in order of appearance, to a well-documented set of resignations.
satire_techniques.effect: Buys the freedom of fiction — interiority, invented scenes, a shaped ending — while keeping the charge of a documented case.
satire_techniques.caution: Deniability is thinner than writers assume, both legally and morally: an invented scene attributed to a recognizable person is an allegation with a novel around it.

satire_techniques.name: the satiric mask drop
satire_techniques.definition: One sincere beat, placed late, where the persona is set down and the writer says plainly what the whole performance has been for.
satire_techniques.example: After nine pages of the costing paper, four sentences in the writer's own voice about the family in paragraph three.
satire_techniques.effect: Converts accumulated comic energy into moral weight, and tells the reader retrospectively how to have read the mask.
satire_techniques.caution: Once, briefly, and at the end. A mask taken off and put back on twice teaches the reader that neither face is the writer's, and a drop that lasts a page is the sermon the satire existed to avoid.

satire_techniques.name: poe's law collapse
satire_techniques.definition: The failure state in which a satire is indistinguishable from a sincere statement of the position it attacks, so that some readers take it straight and circulate it as support.
satire_techniques.example: The costing paper is quoted approvingly in a trade newsletter, with the author's name and without the frame.
satire_techniques.effect: The satire is absorbed as advocacy; every share among the misreading audience does the target's work with the satirist's prose.
satire_techniques.register: any satire that circulates in extract
satire_techniques.caution: The defence is internal, not paratextual: one impossibility, one unignorable excess, one detail that no sincere version of the document could contain. A disclaimer travels less far than the extract does.

satire_techniques.name: clapter
satire_techniques.definition: Satire calibrated to produce agreement rather than laughter — the audience applauds the sentiment because it is theirs, and the joke does no work beyond identifying the side.
satire_techniques.example: A paragraph whose entire mechanism is naming the correct villain, at length, to readers who already dislike him.
satire_techniques.effect: Feels successful in the room and on the page, and changes nothing; the satire has become a membership ritual with punctuation.
satire_techniques.caution: Diagnose by asking what the piece would cost a reader who agrees with it. If the answer is nothing — no discomfort, no implicated party on their own side — it is applause, not satire.

satire_techniques.name: mask slippage
satire_techniques.definition: The unintended failure of an ironic persona: the satirist's own judgement leaks into the impersonated voice through an adjective, an aside or a sentence rhythm the persona would not use.
satire_techniques.example: The costing paper, in its fourth section, calls a proposal callous — a word the Proposer could not have reached for.
satire_techniques.effect: Breaks the reader's trust in the construction; from that point they read for the seams rather than for the argument.
satire_techniques.caution: Distinct from the deliberate mask drop, which is placed and owned. Detect it by reading the persona's prose for evaluative words the persona has no reason to possess.

satire_techniques.name: recuperated satire
satire_techniques.definition: The failure in which the target adopts the satire — quoting it in its own materials, licensing the parody, hiring the satirist — so that the attack becomes evidence of the target's good humour.
satire_techniques.example: The mock policy appears, framed, in the reception area of the department it was written about.
satire_techniques.effect: Converts criticism into a demonstration that the institution can absorb criticism, which is a stronger defence than any rebuttal.
satire_techniques.caution: Recuperability is a property of the piece: satire aimed at manner and style is easily adopted, satire aimed at a specific act with a date and a name is not.

satire_techniques.name: strawman lampoon
satire_techniques.definition: Satirizing a position nobody actually holds, by building the persona out of the writer's opponents' worst-case caricature rather than out of their published words.
satire_techniques.example: A parody memo whose premise is one the department has explicitly rejected in writing, twice.
satire_techniques.effect: Delights readers who already agree and hands the target a free refutation, which is usually the only quotation from the exchange that survives.
satire_techniques.caution: Build the persona out of real quotations before exaggerating; the logical defect belongs to the fallacies file, but the reputational cost lands entirely on the satirist.
